rules.sentence: Standard diagnostic criteria include a mass with distinct echogenicity, well-defined margins, visualization in at least two orthogonal views, and contiguity with an akinetic or dyskinetic segment.

Additional echocardiographic markers of stasis, such as reduced apical longitudinal strain or a low E-wave propagation index (EPI < 1), have shown good sensitivity but limited specificity for thrombus detection.

Contrast TTE significantly improves endocardial border delineation and LV cavity opacification, frequently doubling thrombus detection compared with non-contrast TTE, particularly for mural or laminated thrombi.
CMR is the gold standard for apical LVT detection due to superior spatial resolution and unique tissue characterization potential.
Thrombus appears as a hypointense, non-enhancing mass on LGE imaging; long-inversion-time sequences (~600 ms) markedly improve conspicuity and outperform cine imaging.
LGE burden strongly correlates with thrombus formation, with ischemic cardiomyopathy demonstrating a fivefold increased prevalence compared with non-ischemic disease.
CMR also differentiates thrombus from MVO, the latter being intramyocardial and surrounded by hyperenhancement.
Since prompt anticoagulation for at least three months lowers embolic risk and may affect long-term outcomes, early and accurate identification of LVT is crucial.

Apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (ApHCM), or Yamaguchi syndrome, was first reported in Japan in 1976, and is defined by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy predominantly involving the apex, with an end-diastolic apical wall thickness ≥15 mm.
TTE is the first-line modality for diagnosis and follow-up.
ApHCM typically lacks septal hypertrophy or systolic anterior motion—features that distinguish it from classic HCM—and is generally not associated with LV outflow tract obstruction.
Instead, hypertrophy is confined to the mid-to-apical LV segments, producing the characteristic “ace of spades” configuration.
Apical systolic cavity obliteration, quantified by an end-systolic obliteration ratio >0.5, correlates with adverse prognosis.

Functional assessment with echocardiography shows impaired diastolic filling and reduced apical strain, creating an “inverse-amyloid” deformation pattern; disease progression leads to diminished apical twist and lower global rotational mechanics.
CMR is the preferred modality because of superior apical resolution.
Cine imaging detects hypertrophy and aneurysms—missed by TTE in up to 40% of cases.

LGE burden >15% is associated with increased arrhythmic risk while LGE and T1/T2 mapping characterize fibrosis and help distinguish ApHCM from phenocopies, including Fabry disease (low T1) and cardiac amyloidosis (high T1 and ECV.
